Disengaged citizens who rarely or never discuss politics, have limited political knowledge or interest, and do not feel close to any particular political party.
Rural or less-educated residents with limited internet access who have minimal exposure to political discourse and are uncertain whether they feel close to any party.
Reluctant or non-responsive individuals who refuse to answer political questions or are unwilling to express their political affiliations publicly.

Urban residents with higher media exposure and education who are more likely to have had direct contact with COVID-19 cases or experienced illness themselves, given their greater engagement with news and information networks.

Rural and semi-rural residents with limited healthcare access and lower media engagement who may have experienced COVID-19 illness but didn't seek formal testing or medical confirmation, so they're uncertain whether to report it.

Vaccinated individuals (representing the 45-61% vaccination rate seen in the data) who were more engaged with health information and more likely to have sought testing or medical care if they became ill.

Residents in areas with very limited healthcare infrastructure and testing availability who genuinely did not have access to COVID-19 testing and therefore cannot confirm whether they or household members had the disease.
Individuals who experienced COVID-19 symptoms but attributed them to other common illnesses and did not seek medical attention or testing, so they don't report household illness.

Urban youth with some political awareness who follow government performance and international affairs; they tend to feel connected to political parties that align with their views on governance and development.
Young people with limited political engagement who rarely discuss politics and have minimal awareness of political parties or their platforms; they do not feel close to any particular party.
Youth from areas with lower electricity access and more limited information exposure who lack sufficient knowledge about political parties to feel close to any of them.
Politically disengaged young adults who are aware of parties but deliberately distance themselves from partisan politics, preferring to remain independent.
A small segment of youth who are uncertain about their political affiliations or unwilling to express their party preferences.
Urban internet users with regular news exposure who occasionally discuss politics with friends and family as part of normal social conversation.
People who actively avoid political discussion in social settings, preferring to keep conversations focused on personal, family, or economic matters.
Rural or less connected individuals with limited exposure to political information who rarely if ever engage in political discussions with others.
Socially engaged individuals who frequently discuss political matters and current events when gathering with friends and family.
People uncertain about their discussion patterns or reluctant to characterize their social conversations regarding politics.
Urban and peri-urban residents with better infrastructure access who have water sources inside their homes or compounds, reflecting modern water supply systems in more developed areas.
Rural and semi-rural residents who rely on water sources outside their compounds, such as communal boreholes, wells, or natural water points, which is common in less densely populated areas.
Residents in transitional areas with mixed access who have water inside their compounds but not inside their houses, representing intermediate infrastructure development.
Residents with very limited water access or those in remote areas where water availability is a significant challenge and sources are distant from their homes.

Politically engaged citizens who actively follow government affairs and regularly discuss political corruption, development assistance, and governance with family and friends; they view political discussion as an important civic duty.

Moderately interested citizens who occasionally bring up political topics when gathered with others, particularly regarding economic hardship and government performance, but don't seek out these conversations.

Economically stressed individuals dealing with irregular cash income who focus conversations on survival and practical family matters rather than abstract political discussion, though they may comment on government handling of corruption when prompted.
Politically disengaged citizens who rarely or never discuss political matters with friends and family, viewing such conversations as unimportant or preferring to avoid conflict in social settings.
Cautious individuals who are uncertain about political engagement and may refuse to discuss or admit to discussing political matters due to concerns about safety or social consequences.

Skeptical citizens with direct experience of corruption: People who have personally encountered or witnessed government corruption, particularly regarding cash income and economic opportunities. Disengaged or uninformed citizens: People with limited access to information about government anti-corruption efforts, either due to lack of electricity (69% lack connections), limited media exposure, or focus on immediate survival needs. Politically engaged party supporters: People who feel close to a political party (61% do) and discuss politics occasionally or frequently with others. Government defenders or loyalists: A small segment who believe the current government is making genuine efforts against corruption and view it as handling the issue fairly or very well, often aligned with their political party affiliation.
Economically stressed youth with limited resources who rarely engage in political discussion, viewing it as a luxury or distraction from daily survival concerns
Socially active young adults in urban or semi-urban areas who occasionally discuss politics with friends and family as part of casual social conversation
Politically engaged youth, often more educated or with access to media, who frequently discuss political matters and governance issues with their social circles
Disengaged youth who avoid political discussion due to skepticism about government effectiveness or concerns about safety in expressing political views
Community-oriented young adults in rural areas who occasionally discuss local political and governance matters within family settings but less frequently in broader social contexts

Pessimists about national direction who believe the country is going in the wrong direction, likely influenced by concerns about corruption (which 40-36% view as being handled very badly) and general dissatisfaction with governance.
Cautious optimists or those with mixed views who believe the country is going in the right direction, possibly seeing some government efforts or maintaining hope despite challenges.
Disengaged citizens who don't know or are uncertain about the country's direction, reflecting the pattern of high 'don't know' responses (42% on Japan assistance question) common in this group.
Politically engaged individuals who feel close to a party (38-74% range in previous data) and have formed opinions about national direction based on partisan perspectives.
Those who refuse to answer or are unwilling to express views on the country's direction, though refusal rates are typically very low in this population.

Urban professionals and educated individuals with exposure to international news and development discourse through media, work, or education. They are aware of Japan's development assistance programs in Kenya.

Politically engaged urban residents who follow current affairs and political discussions regularly. They have some awareness of foreign aid and international relations but may have limited specific knowledge about Japan's role.

General urban population with moderate media consumption and basic awareness of international matters. They have vague familiarity with the concept of foreign assistance but cannot confirm Japan's specific involvement.
Urban residents with limited engagement in news and international affairs, primarily focused on local concerns. They have not encountered information about Japan's development assistance.
A small segment that actively avoids or refuses to engage with questions about international relations and foreign policy matters.
Urban youth with regular internet access who use the internet daily for social media, messaging, and news consumption, primarily in cities like Niamey.
Young people with moderate internet access who use it several times a week when they can afford data or find WiFi, balancing online and offline activities.
Rural or economically disadvantaged youth with very limited internet access who rarely or never use the internet due to lack of infrastructure, affordability, or electricity.
Occasional internet users who access it less than once a month when they have specific needs or opportunities, representing those with sporadic connectivity.
Youth with minimal digital literacy or interest who have never used the internet despite living in areas with some connectivity.

Highly trusting relatives-focused individuals who prioritize family bonds as their primary social safety net. They express strong trust in relatives, viewing family as the most reliable institution in an uncertain economic environment.

Moderately trusting individuals who value family relationships but maintain some caution based on personal experiences. They trust relatives substantially but acknowledge occasional disappointments or limitations in family support.

Cautious individuals with mixed experiences in family relationships who express qualified trust in relatives. They trust some family members more than others and are aware of potential conflicts or unreliability within extended family networks.

Skeptical individuals with limited family support systems or difficult family histories who express minimal trust in relatives. They may have experienced family breakdown, migration, or economic strain that has eroded family bonds.
Non-responsive individuals who decline to answer or express uncertainty about their trust in relatives. They may be uncomfortable discussing family matters or lack clear family structures.

Urban, internet-daily users with higher education and political engagement. They follow international news and are aware of major development partnerships, including Japan's role in African development assistance.

Occasional internet users with moderate education living in urban or semi-urban areas. They have some awareness of international relations but their knowledge of specific countries' aid programs is limited and patchy.
Rural or low-connectivity residents with limited internet access and minimal exposure to international news. They have little to no knowledge of Japan's development assistance to Côte d'Ivoire.

Individuals with some secondary education and occasional news consumption through radio or community discussion. They may have heard vague references to foreign aid but cannot confirm specifics about Japan.

Highly educated professionals or government/business sector workers with regular international engagement. They are well-informed about Japan's significant development partnerships and loan programs in West Africa.

Religiously committed Christians who view their faith as central to identity and are cautious about close relationships with people of different religions, seeing potential spiritual or moral concerns.
Moderate Christians who are comfortable with people of different religions as neighbors but may have some reservations, viewing religious difference as acceptable in a diverse society.
Inclusive Christians who actively welcome people of different religions as neighbors and see religious diversity as enriching, reflecting cosmopolitan or urban values.
Pragmatic Christians who don't particularly care about neighbors' religion and focus on practical qualities like trustworthiness and neighborliness regardless of faith.
Highly conservative Christians with strong religious convictions who strongly dislike the idea of neighbors from different religions, viewing it as incompatible with their faith commitments.

Disengaged and uninformed citizens who rarely consume news (76% never watch TV) and haven't heard enough about government corruption efforts to form an opinion. They default to 'Don't Know' due to limited information exposure.

Skeptical critics who believe the government is handling corruption very badly, reflecting broader frustration with governance in Zimbabwe. They have some news exposure and hold strong negative views.

Moderately critical citizens who think the government is handling corruption fairly badly, representing those with some awareness but not extreme pessimism. They occupy a middle-ground skeptical position.

Cautious optimists or government supporters who believe the government is handling corruption fairly well or very well. This is a small minority, possibly reflecting either genuine belief in anti-corruption efforts or political alignment.
Refusers who decline to answer, potentially due to political sensitivity or fear of expressing criticism in Zimbabwe's context. This represents a small but notable segment.

Urban residents with higher education and media exposure who are more aware of COVID-19 cases through television and news sources; they are more likely to have personally experienced or known someone affected by COVID-19.
Rural or semi-rural residents with limited media access who have had minimal direct contact with confirmed COVID-19 cases; they may be unaware of cases in their community despite potential exposure.
Individuals in informal employment or economic hardship who experienced COVID-19 illness but did not seek testing or formal diagnosis; they may not report it as a confirmed case.
Health-conscious individuals who actively follow news and health information and are more likely to have sought testing if symptomatic; they have clearer awareness of their COVID-19 status.
Skeptical or mistrustful respondents who doubt COVID-19's severity or existence in their community and are unlikely to report illness as COVID-related even if symptomatic.

Rural farmers and agricultural workers with limited formal education who have minimal exposure to international affairs and development assistance programs. They are unlikely to have heard about Japanese loans or assistance.

Local government officials, teachers, and community leaders who have some awareness of national development initiatives and international partnerships through their work or media exposure. They may have heard about Japanese assistance but lack detailed knowledge.

Younger, more educated individuals with access to television and some engagement with news who are aware that Senegal receives development assistance from various countries including Japan. They can provide a more informed answer.
Older community members and elders who may have historical knowledge of Japanese presence or assistance in Senegal from past decades but are uncertain about current programs.
Individuals who are uncertain or cautious about answering questions regarding international relations and foreign assistance, preferring to express uncertainty rather than guess.
Daily television news consumers who rely on TV as their primary news source, reflecting the traditional media consumption pattern still dominant in Zimbabwe despite internet growth.
Moderate television users who watch a few times a week, balancing traditional TV news with occasional internet use, representing those with some media diversification.
Infrequent television users who rarely engage with TV news, preferring internet-based news sources despite the digital divide, particularly among younger or more urban-oriented individuals.
Non-television news consumers who never watch TV for news, relying entirely on internet or other alternative sources, a smaller but growing segment in the unemployed/job-seeking demographic.
Occasional or uncertain television users with sporadic engagement, including those with limited access or inconsistent viewing habits due to economic constraints.
Daily television news consumers, primarily older and rural residents who rely on TV as their main news source and watch news every day
Regular but not daily TV news watchers, urban and semi-urban residents who check television news several times a week as part of their routine
Occasional television news consumers who get news from TV a few times a month, often younger people who supplement TV with internet sources
Minimal TV news users who rarely or never watch television for news, typically younger urban residents who prefer internet-based news sources
Non-respondents and those uncertain about their TV news consumption patterns
Cosmopolitan urbanites and educated professionals who interact regularly with people from different ethnic groups and view such diversity neutrally or positively as normal and enriching.
Pragmatic community members who accept people from other ethnic groups as neighbors without strong feelings either way, viewing coexistence as practical and unremarkable.
Traditionalists with some ethnic preference who would somewhat dislike having neighbors from other ethnic groups, though not with intense opposition.
Strong ethnic identifiers who strongly dislike the idea of neighbors from other ethnic groups, viewing their own ethnic community as distinctly preferable.
Uncertain or non-responsive individuals who either don't know how they feel about this question or prefer not to answer directly.
Conservative Muslims and traditionalists (majority) who view homosexuality as incompatible with Islamic and cultural values, and strongly oppose it as neighbors
Pragmatic moderates who have reservations about homosexuality but focus on practical coexistence and would tolerate it without strong feelings
Urban, educated, internet-connected individuals (small minority) who hold more liberal views on personal freedoms and would not care or somewhat accept homosexual neighbors
Rural and less-educated populations with limited exposure to diverse perspectives who are uncertain or indifferent due to lack of familiarity with the issue
Individuals who refuse to answer or express uncertainty due to social sensitivity around the topic

Strongly accepting Christians and Muslims who emphasize religious tolerance and coexistence. They have regular contact with people of different faiths in their rural communities and view religious diversity positively.
Moderately accepting individuals who would not mind having neighbors of different religions but don't strongly prefer it. They are neutral or slightly positive on religious diversity.

Conservative religious adherents who are somewhat uncomfortable with religious differences but accept them as a practical reality in their communities. They tolerate but don't enthusiastically welcome religious diversity.
Strongly religious individuals with more rigid views who actively dislike the idea of neighbors from different religions. They see religious boundaries as important and prefer religious homogeneity.
A small group uncertain or unwilling to express their views on religious neighbors, either due to social sensitivity or genuine ambivalence.
Deeply disillusioned citizens who see pervasive government corruption and lack of development in rural areas, feeling the country is fundamentally on the wrong track
Cautiously pessimistic residents who acknowledge some government efforts but remain skeptical about real progress and direction, leaning toward wrong direction
Pragmatic optimists who see modest improvements or potential in current government initiatives despite challenges, believing the country is moving in the right direction
Uncertain or disengaged individuals with limited information about national affairs, unable to form a clear judgment about the country's direction
Rural residents with strong faith in government leadership or recent local development projects, firmly convinced the country is going in the right direction

Politically disengaged women with limited political discussion and awareness. They rarely discuss politics with others and have low knowledge of international relations, making them unlikely to feel close to any party.

Women with regular internet access and occasional political engagement. They discuss politics occasionally and have moderate awareness of current affairs, but still maintain distance from formal party affiliation.
Politically active women who frequently discuss politics with friends and family. They are more informed and engaged, and are more likely to identify with a particular political party.
Women uncertain about their political alignment or the political landscape. They lack clear knowledge about parties and their positions, leading them to express uncertainty rather than commitment.
Women who actively refuse to disclose their political party affiliation due to privacy concerns or political sensitivity in their environment.
Urban residents with stable housing and moderate income who have indoor plumbing installed in their homes, viewing toilet access as a basic necessity they have secured.
Rural and peri-urban residents with modest means who have constructed pit latrines or basic toilet facilities within their compound boundaries as a practical solution.
Lower-income households in informal settlements or rural areas who rely on shared or communal toilet facilities located outside their compounds due to space and financial constraints.
Economically disadvantaged individuals in remote rural areas who lack access to any toilet or latrine facility and practice open defecation.
A small segment of respondents uncertain about their household's sanitation situation or unwilling to disclose details about their toilet access.
Urban residents with regular internet access who are more aware of COVID-19 cases and health information, and more likely to have encountered the virus directly or know someone who did.

Rural or semi-rural residents with limited internet access who have had minimal direct exposure to COVID-19 cases and rely on local community knowledge, making them less likely to report personal or household illness.
Older adults or those in vulnerable health categories who may have experienced COVID-19 illness but may not have sought testing or formal diagnosis due to limited healthcare access.
Younger, more educated individuals in urban areas who are more likely to have been tested and confirmed positive, and therefore more aware of their COVID-19 status.
Individuals who are hesitant about COVID-19 or skeptical of the pandemic's severity, and therefore unlikely to report illness even if they experienced symptoms.

Urban professionals and daily internet users with stable employment. They have consistent cash income and rarely experience financial hardship, viewing income security as a normal part of their economic life.

Rural and semi-urban residents with irregular income sources (agriculture, informal work, small business). They experience periodic cash shortages, typically going without income just once or twice yearly during seasonal downturns or business fluctuations.
Chronically poor or unemployed individuals with minimal income sources. They experience persistent cash income problems many times per year or constantly, struggling with severe economic instability.

Politically engaged citizens (those close to parties) with mixed economic circumstances. Their experience with cash income shortages varies widely depending on employment sector and regional economic conditions, distributed across the other categories.
Daily internet users, primarily younger and urban-based individuals who rely on the internet for news, work, and communication. They represent the digitally connected segment of Cameroonian society.
Occasional internet users (few times a week to few times a month) who access the internet for specific purposes but are not dependent on it daily. They balance online and offline information sources.

Minimal internet users (less than once a month or never) from rural areas or lower socioeconomic backgrounds with limited digital infrastructure access or digital literacy. They primarily rely on traditional media and word-of-mouth.

Politically engaged individuals across all internet usage levels who actively seek news and discuss current events, including government performance and national direction. They tend to be more critical of governance issues.

Socially cohesive individuals who prioritize community harmony and are generally accepting of ethnic and religious diversity as neighbors, regardless of their internet usage patterns. They represent the inclusive social fabric of Cameroonian society.

Urban residents with stable employment in Seychelles' developed infrastructure sectors (tourism, government, services). They have reliable electricity access and view it as a basic utility they depend on daily.

Rural or semi-rural residents and those in less developed areas of the islands. They may have electricity access but it could be less reliable, or they may lack it entirely, viewing it as a service they struggle to access consistently.

Residents in newly developed or recently upgraded areas of Seychelles. They have gained electricity access relatively recently and are aware of the infrastructure improvements happening in their country.
Older residents or those in isolated island communities. They may lack electricity connection or have only partial access, and view electrification as a luxury rather than a standard utility.
Residents uncertain about their situation or unwilling to answer directly. They may be confused about what counts as an 'electric connection' or prefer not to disclose their infrastructure status.

Urban internet-connected professionals with stable employment. These individuals have regular cash income and rarely experience financial hardship; they view cash income security as a normal part of their economic life.

Rural and semi-rural residents with inconsistent income from agriculture or informal work. They experience periodic cash shortages tied to seasonal patterns and market conditions, going without cash income several times per year.

Informal sector workers and day laborers in urban areas with highly variable income. They frequently face gaps in cash income and struggle with unpredictable earnings, experiencing cash shortages many times throughout the year.

Unemployed or underemployed individuals with minimal economic safety nets. They experience chronic cash income shortages and may go without cash income for extended periods, reflecting persistent economic vulnerability.

Small business owners and traders with moderate but fluctuating income. They occasionally experience cash flow disruptions but generally maintain some income stability, going without cash only once or twice per year.

Urban residents and service workers without personal vehicle ownership. They rely on public transportation or informal transit options and see motor vehicles as expensive assets beyond their current reach, though some may have family members who own motorcycles for commercial purposes.

Rural and semi-rural residents with modest incomes who own motorcycles or small motor vehicles for agricultural work, trading, or transportation. They view vehicle ownership as a practical necessity for their livelihoods rather than a luxury.

Established business owners and traders with stable cash income who personally own motor vehicles or motorcycles as tools for their commercial activities. They see vehicle ownership as integral to maintaining their economic status.

Younger adults and recent migrants in urban areas who aspire to vehicle ownership but currently cannot afford it, though they may occasionally use family members' vehicles. They recognize vehicle ownership as a marker of economic progress.
Individuals with limited awareness or engagement with the survey question who provide minimal responses. They represent a small portion of the group with unclear ownership situations.

Urban/peri-urban residents with improved water access. These young people have water sources within or very close to their homes, reflecting Kenya's urban infrastructure development and their group's relatively higher socioeconomic status compared to older age groups.

Rural residents with compound-level water access. These individuals rely on water sources located within their compound but not inside the house, a common arrangement in rural Kenya where boreholes or communal taps serve household clusters.

Residents with limited water access outside the compound. These young people must fetch water from sources beyond their immediate compound, indicating more constrained circumstances, though this group is smaller than in older age cohorts.

Uncertain or non-responsive individuals. A small segment either doesn't know where their main water source is located or refuses to answer, reflecting either genuine ambiguity about water access or survey participation hesitancy.
Vaccine-hesitant individuals who have not been vaccinated, skeptical of COVID-19 vaccines due to limited access, misinformation, or general distrust of health interventions.
Vaccinated urban residents with better access to healthcare facilities and information, who received one or more COVID-19 doses through government or private health programs.
Rural residents with limited vaccine access who have not been vaccinated due to geographic barriers and lack of healthcare infrastructure despite potential willingness.
Cautious individuals who are aware of COVID-19 but uncertain about vaccination, neither strongly opposed nor actively seeking vaccines.
Individuals who refuse to answer or are unsure about their vaccination status, representing a small segment with privacy concerns or unclear vaccination history.

Pragmatic coexistence majority: People who live in ethnically mixed communities and interact regularly with other ethnic groups out of necessity and daily life. They view people from other ethnic groups neutrally or positively as neighbors.
Warm welcomers: People with positive attitudes toward ethnic diversity who actively appreciate having neighbors from different ethnic backgrounds and see it as enriching.
Cautious skeptics: People who have some reservations about ethnic differences but don't strongly oppose having neighbors from other ethnic groups, preferring to maintain some social distance.
Ethnic preference holders: People who somewhat dislike the idea of neighbors from other ethnic groups, though this view is not strongly held or expressed.
Strong ethnic exclusionists: People who strongly dislike the prospect of neighbors from other ethnic groups, though this represents a very small minority in the group.

Urban professionals with high daily internet use who are cosmopolitan and trusting. These individuals are digitally connected, engage regularly with diverse information sources, and maintain open attitudes toward people from other ethnic groups, extending this openness to strong trust in their relatives.

Regular news consumers (TV and internet) with moderate internet engagement who are socially integrated. They consume news daily through traditional and digital channels, are comfortable with ethnic diversity, and express solid trust in family relationships as a core social institution.

Selective internet users with lower daily connectivity who are somewhat cautious but family-oriented. They use the internet less frequently than the urban average, rely more on television for news, and while open to diversity, they place particular emphasis on family trust as their primary social anchor.

Limited digital engagement individuals who rarely use the internet for news or daily purposes. They represent the segment with minimal online connectivity but still maintain positive views toward ethnic diversity; they tend toward strong family trust as their most reliable social relationship.

Politically engaged discussants who frequently talk about politics with family and friends. Regardless of their internet usage patterns, these individuals are more socially aware and tend to have thoughtful, nuanced views on trust relationships, including measured but genuine confidence in relatives.
Urban residents with better healthcare access and higher education who are more likely to have sought testing and received medical care, making them aware of COVID-19 infections in their household.

Rural residents with limited healthcare infrastructure and testing availability who experienced COVID-19 symptoms but never tested positive, so they don't report confirmed cases despite likely exposure.
Economically vulnerable households experiencing cash income instability who lack resources for healthcare visits or testing, and therefore have no confirmed diagnosis despite potential infections.
Relatively better-off households with access to healthcare and testing who can confirm whether household members contracted COVID-19, representing the minority with documented cases.
Individuals with strong community networks and health literacy who actively sought information about COVID-19 and pursued testing when symptomatic, enabling them to report confirmed infections.

Urban professionals and educated individuals with exposure to international news and development issues. They are aware of Japan's development assistance programs in Angola and can identify Japan as a donor country.

Rural and less-educated citizens with limited access to media and international information. They have not heard about Japanese development assistance and are genuinely uncertain about Japan's role in Angola.

Politically engaged citizens who follow government and international affairs closely. They know about Japan's loans and development assistance to Angola through government announcements or news coverage.
Younger, digitally-connected individuals in urban areas who may have some awareness of international development but are not deeply informed about specific donor countries' activities.
Citizens who are skeptical or disengaged from information about government and international relations. They either refuse to answer or are unwilling to engage with the question.

Wage earners with stable employment who feel financially secure. These individuals, representing the majority of the group with regular salaries, generally report living comfortably or coping adequately on their present income.

Working-age employed individuals experiencing moderate financial strain. Despite having wages or self-employment income, they find it difficult to manage on their current income due to household expenses or economic pressures.

Pensioners and older adults with fixed retirement income. This group, representing a significant minority, tends to report coping or experiencing difficulty depending on pension adequacy and household composition.
Self-employed individuals and small business owners with variable income. They show mixed views on financial comfort, ranging from those doing well to those struggling with income volatility.

Households experiencing severe financial hardship. A smaller segment reports very difficult circumstances, likely including those with unemployment benefits, social support, or multiple dependents on limited income.

Religious conservatives in the village who hold traditional values and believe religious principles should guide social norms; they tend to strongly disagree that gay people should be free to live as they wish.

Moderate traditionalists with some religious affiliation who have reservations about homosexuality but recognize individual freedoms; they are more likely to disagree or remain neutral rather than strongly oppose.
Pragmatic villagers with mixed views who neither strongly support nor oppose LGBTQ+ freedoms, reflecting uncertainty or indifference on the issue.
Progressive-minded residents who believe in personal freedom and equality regardless of sexual orientation; they agree that gay people should be free to live as they wish.
Strong advocates for LGBTQ+ rights and personal liberty who firmly believe gay men and lesbians should have complete freedom to live their lives without restriction.

Traditional married individuals who have maintained conventional family structures throughout their lives and view cohabitation without marriage as inconsistent with their values, though they show moderate tolerance toward others' choices.
Secular or liberal-leaning individuals who have personally experienced cohabitation and approve of non-marital partnerships, viewing them as legitimate lifestyle choices equivalent to marriage.
Pragmatic individuals who may have cohabited in the past or present but hold somewhat ambivalent views, neither strongly approving nor disapproving of the practice.
Religious or socially conservative individuals who disapprove of cohabitation without marriage on principle and have not personally engaged in such arrangements.
Younger-minded or progressive individuals within this age cohort who actively support cohabitation as a valid alternative to marriage and may have experienced it themselves.

Pragmatic acceptors (largest group): People who have lived with unmarried partners themselves or are comfortable with modern relationship arrangements. They approve of having children outside marriage as a practical reality of contemporary life.
Neutral moderates: People who neither strongly approve nor disapprove of unmarried couples having children. They see it as a personal choice without strong moral judgment either way.
Cautious disapprovers: People with traditional values who believe marriage should precede childbearing, though they're not strongly opposed. They disapprove but recognize this is increasingly common.
Strong traditionalists: People who strongly disapprove of having children outside marriage on moral or religious grounds. They view marriage as a prerequisite for family formation.
Enthusiastic progressives: People who actively approve of the freedom for couples to have children regardless of marital status. They see this as a positive expression of personal autonomy.

Working-class individuals in stable employment, often in manufacturing, construction, or service sectors. They view trade union membership as a practical way to protect worker rights and negotiate better wages and conditions, and many are currently or have been members.
Older workers who were union members during their careers but are now retired or no longer in the workforce. They have previous union experience but are no longer active members.

Self-employed workers, small business owners, or those in informal employment who have never joined a union and see little relevance to their work situation. They view unions as primarily for traditional employees.

Younger or precarious workers in gig economy, temporary, or low-wage service jobs who are aware of unions but face barriers to membership or lack strong union presence in their sectors. They are skeptical about union effectiveness for their situation.

Individuals with limited awareness or engagement with labor organization issues who have never considered union membership as relevant to their lives. They simply have no experience with or knowledge of unions.

Non-unionized workers and service sector employees in small towns who have never joined a union, viewing them as less relevant to their work situation or having limited exposure to union organizing in their local area.
Former union members, typically older workers or those who were in manufacturing or public sector jobs earlier in their careers but are no longer actively involved in union activities.
Current union members, primarily in public sector, education, or traditional industries who maintain active membership and see unions as important for workplace protections and collective bargaining.

Young professionals and self-employed individuals in small towns who work in modern sectors (services, retail, small businesses) where union membership is uncommon and not part of their professional culture.
Skeptical non-members who are aware of unions but consciously choose not to join due to ideological views, perceived ineffectiveness, or preference for individual negotiation.
Secular progressives with strong liberal values who actively reject religious identification, viewing religion as incompatible with modern secular society.
Non-religious pragmatists who don't identify with religion but aren't ideologically opposed to it; they simply don't see it as relevant to their lives.
Cultural Catholics who maintain nominal religious identification as part of Belgian cultural heritage and family tradition, even if not actively practicing.
Committed religious believers (Catholic, Protestant, or other denominations) for whom faith is an important part of their identity and worldview.
Immigrants and religious minorities who identify strongly with their faith community as a source of cultural identity and social belonging.

Socially liberal individuals who strongly reject traditional stigma around homosexuality. Having internalized progressive values about sexual orientation, they would firmly disagree with feeling ashamed of a gay family member.

Moderately tolerant people who accept homosexuality as normal but may retain some residual discomfort. They would disagree with the shame statement, though perhaps less emphatically than the first group.
Conflicted individuals who hold mixed views, neither fully accepting nor rejecting homosexuality. They would neither agree nor disagree, reflecting genuine ambivalence about family acceptance.

Traditionally-minded people who maintain conservative views on sexuality and family values. They would agree that they would feel some shame, viewing homosexuality as inconsistent with their moral framework.

Strongly conservative individuals with deeply held religious or traditional beliefs who would strongly agree they would feel ashamed. This represents the most resistant segment to changing attitudes on this issue.
Religious traditionalists with strong Catholic faith. They view religious identity as a fundamental and non-negotiable part of their personal and cultural identity, deeply rooted in Polish tradition.

Secular or non-religious individuals who have consciously distanced themselves from organized religion. They do not identify with any religious denomination and view religion as unnecessary for their lives.

Culturally Catholic but religiously indifferent people who maintain nominal religious identity for social or family reasons rather than genuine belief. They acknowledge religious affiliation without active practice or conviction.

Agnostic or questioning individuals who are uncertain about religious matters and prefer not to commit to a specific religious identity. They remain open to spiritual questions but do not affiliate with denominations.

Members of minority religious communities (Orthodox, Protestant, or other faiths). They identify strongly with their specific religious denomination, though they represent a very small portion of the population.

Religiously engaged community members with limited formal education who view civic participation through traditional community and church networks rather than formal petition signing; they see petitions as less relevant to how they effect change.

Socially progressive individuals with less than lower secondary education who support LGBTQ+ rights and are more inclined toward modern forms of civic engagement like petition signing, seeing it as an accessible way to voice concerns.
Disengaged or skeptical citizens with minimal education who rarely participate in any civic activities, whether traditional or modern, and see petitions as ineffective or not relevant to their lives.
Pragmatic working-age individuals who occasionally engage in civic activities and might sign petitions on issues directly affecting them or their families, though such engagement is sporadic.
Marginally active community members who have engaged in some organizational work or boycotts but remain largely disconnected from formal petition-signing as a mode of civic participation.
Secular progressives with strong support for LGBTQ+ rights. They strongly disagree with the statement and feel no shame about having a gay family member, viewing such attitudes as outdated prejudice.
Religious moderates who are accepting despite their faith background. They disagree with the statement, having reconciled their religious beliefs with acceptance of LGBTQ+ family members.
Ambivalent middle-grounders with some traditional values but not strongly opposed. They neither agree nor disagree, reflecting uncertainty or discomfort with the topic without outright rejection.

Conservative traditionalists with religious or cultural reservations. They agree with the statement to some degree, feeling genuine discomfort or shame about having a gay family member due to their values.

Strong traditionalists with deep religious conviction or cultural opposition. They strongly agree that they would feel ashamed, viewing homosexuality as fundamentally incompatible with their worldview.

Politically engaged older citizens who remain active in civic participation despite their age. They view petition-signing as a legitimate and accessible way to express their views on issues they care about.
Moderately civically minded retirees who occasionally engage in low-effort activism like petitions when they feel strongly about specific issues, but don't make it a regular practice.
Traditionally-oriented older adults who prefer established institutional channels (voting, direct contact with representatives) over petition-signing, viewing it as less formal or effective.
Socially withdrawn or disengaged seniors who have largely stepped back from civic activities and see petition-signing as not relevant to their lives.

Health-limited or digitally disconnected older citizens who would support causes but face practical barriers to signing petitions, whether due to mobility issues or unfamiliarity with petition platforms.
Practicing Catholics with strong religious identity. These individuals maintain active faith commitments and see religion as central to their personal and family life.
Culturally religious but non-practicing. They identify with Catholicism as part of Polish heritage and tradition but do not actively practice or attend services regularly.
Secular or non-religious individuals. They have consciously distanced themselves from religious identification and do not consider themselves part of any denomination.
Indifferent or ambivalent about religion. They have not given the question much thought and may drift between identifying and not identifying depending on context.
Members of minority faiths or alternative spiritual movements. A very small segment identifying with non-Catholic denominations or other religious traditions.

Socially liberal urbanites (often younger, more educated): Strongly disagree with the statement, viewing family acceptance of LGBTQ+ members as a moral imperative and seeing shame as outdated prejudice.
Pragmatic moderates: Disagree or feel neutral, believing that while traditional values matter, family bonds and personal acceptance should transcend sexual orientation.
Traditional conservatives with some tolerance: Neither agree nor disagree or mildly disagree, uncomfortable with homosexuality but not willing to openly endorse shame toward family members.
Conservative traditionalists: Agree that they would feel ashamed, viewing homosexuality as conflicting with religious or cultural values, though this represents a minority position.
Strongly opposed to LGBTQ+ acceptance: Strongly agree with the statement, holding firm traditional or religious convictions that make family acceptance of homosexuality deeply problematic.

Pragmatic acceptors: Legally married themselves, but hold liberal views on cohabitation. They see living together without marriage as a reasonable modern choice and approve of it, having likely experienced or considered such arrangements themselves.

Neutral moderates: Legally married Austrians who neither strongly approve nor disapprove of cohabitation. They view it as a personal choice that doesn't concern them much, reflecting a live-and-let-live attitude.

Traditional skeptics: Legally married individuals who disapprove of cohabitation without marriage, viewing it as morally or socially problematic. They believe marriage is the proper foundation for shared living arrangements.

Strong progressives: Legally married but holding very liberal views, strongly approving of cohabitation as equally valid to marriage. They see marriage as optional and cohabitation as a legitimate lifestyle choice.
Disapproving traditionalists: Legally married individuals who strongly disapprove of unmarried cohabitation, viewing it as contrary to traditional values and proper social order.
Non-unionized private sector workers and self-employed individuals who have never joined a trade union, viewing them as unnecessary or irrelevant to their work situation.
Former union members from manufacturing or industrial backgrounds who were previously unionized but have since left the workforce or changed sectors, retaining some awareness of union benefits.
Current public sector or industrial workers who maintain active union membership, seeing it as important for workplace protection and collective bargaining.
Young professionals and service sector workers with upper secondary education who are skeptical of unions due to Italy's economic conditions and labor market fragmentation.
Older workers in traditional industries who have long-standing union membership and view it as a fundamental part of their professional identity.
Working-class and rural Russians with limited exposure to consumer activism; they view boycotts as irrelevant to their daily concerns and lack awareness of such practices.
Older, traditionally-oriented Russians with Soviet-era attitudes who see boycotts as Western political activism incompatible with Russian values and state interests.
Urban professionals and younger educated Russians who engage in selective product boycotts for ethical or political reasons, though this remains a minority practice.
Trade union members and politically active Russians who may boycott products as part of organized labor or nationalist campaigns against foreign brands.
Religiously observant Russians who avoid certain products for moral or religious reasons, viewing this as consistent with their faith rather than political activism.
Traditional married Catholics and conservatives who have never cohabited and view unmarried cohabitation as morally wrong or inappropriate, reflecting strong disapproval of this lifestyle choice.
Pragmatic moderates who have never lived with a partner but hold neutral or mildly accepting views toward cohabitation, seeing it as a personal choice without strong moral judgment.
Experienced cohabitants who lived with a partner before marriage or in a civil union and approve of cohabitation based on their own positive experience.
Secular progressives who approve of cohabitation as a valid lifestyle choice and may have lived with partners themselves, viewing it as a modern and acceptable alternative to marriage.
Divorced or separated individuals who cohabited previously and hold accepting views toward unmarried partnerships based on their life experience.

Secular progressives with strong liberal values who actively reject religious identification and embrace secular worldviews. They align with the group's strong support for LGBTQ+ rights and tend to be skeptical of organized religion.

Non-religious pragmatists who don't identify with religion but aren't ideologically opposed to it; they simply don't see it as relevant to their lives. They represent a secular but non-activist segment.

Cultural Catholics or nominal believers who maintain some religious identification tied to Belgian cultural tradition and family heritage, even if they don't practice actively. They tend to hold moderate social views.

Committed religious believers who actively identify with their faith community and see religion as important to their identity and values. They represent a smaller but meaningful religious minority in the group.
Socially progressive believers who reconcile religious identity with liberal values on issues like LGBTQ+ rights, representing the intersection of faith and progressive politics.
Pragmatic acceptors who have cohabited themselves (or are open to it). They see cohabitation as a normal, practical arrangement and approve of the freedom to live with a partner without marriage.
Neutral moderates with no strong feelings either way. They neither approve nor disapprove of cohabitation, viewing it as a personal choice that doesn't warrant judgment.
Traditional conservatives who disapprove of cohabitation on moral or religious grounds. They believe marriage should precede living together and view cohabitation as undermining family values.
Cautious acceptors who approve of cohabitation but with some reservations. They see it as acceptable in modern society while maintaining some traditional concerns about unmarried partnerships.
Strong disapprovers who strongly reject cohabitation as morally wrong. They hold firm traditional or religious views that cohabitation is inappropriate regardless of circumstances.

Engaged middle-class professionals and employees with stable incomes who actively participate in community and professional organisations. They see organisational involvement as a normal part of civic life and social responsibility.

Working-age employees focused primarily on their jobs and immediate family responsibilities, with limited time or inclination for additional organisational involvement. They view such participation as optional rather than essential.

Retired individuals with pensions and more available time, some of whom channel this into voluntary work and organisational participation while others prefer leisure activities. Their engagement varies considerably based on personal interests and health.

Socially isolated or economically constrained individuals with limited social networks and fewer resources to participate in organisations. They see organisational involvement as something for others rather than themselves.

Religiously or community-minded individuals who participate in faith-based or local organisations as an extension of their values and social identity. They view such involvement as integral to their sense of belonging.

Urban progressives and cohabitation-experienced Finns who have lived with partners outside marriage. They view cohabitation as a normal, accepted life choice and are comfortable with non-traditional relationship arrangements.

Moderate centrists with traditional leanings who have not cohabited but accept it as a valid choice for others. They are neither strongly opposed nor enthusiastically supportive of unmarried cohabitation.

Conservative or religiously-oriented Finns who have never lived with a partner outside marriage and prefer traditional marital structures. They disapprove of cohabitation but are not extremely vocal about it.
Pragmatic middle-ground Finns who may have cohabited or considered it, viewing it as a practical arrangement rather than a moral statement. They are indifferent to the marital status question.

Strongly traditional Finns who view cohabitation as morally problematic and prefer marriage as the only appropriate framework for shared living. They have not cohabited and actively disapprove of the practice.

Progressive urban women who strongly reject traditional stigma around homosexuality. They would strongly disagree with feeling ashamed of having a gay family member, viewing such shame as outdated and contrary to personal freedom.
Socially liberal women with modern values who disagree with the statement. They accept LGBTQ+ family members naturally, though they may not be as vocally activist as the first group.

Women with mixed or uncertain views who neither strongly agree nor disagree. They may feel some traditional social discomfort but recognize it as problematic, or they simply haven't formed strong opinions on the matter.

Conservative women influenced by traditional or religious values who would agree they might feel some shame. They hold more conventional views on family and sexuality, though this group is relatively small in Czech society.

Women with strong traditional convictions who would strongly agree with feeling ashamed. They maintain conservative views on homosexuality and family honor, representing the smallest segment of this group.

Conservative traditionalists with lower education who strongly oppose same-sex adoption on religious or traditional family values grounds. They view traditional family structures as essential for child welfare.
Pragmatic moderates who have reservations about same-sex adoption but aren't strongly opposed. They may worry about practical concerns or social acceptance but aren't ideologically rigid.
Socially liberal individuals with lower secondary education who support equal rights for same-sex couples in adoption. They believe sexual orientation shouldn't determine parental fitness.
Ambivalent or uncertain respondents who genuinely have no strong opinion on this issue and sit in the middle, perhaps due to limited exposure to the topic or conflicting values.
Strongly progressive advocates who firmly agree that same-sex couples deserve equal adoption rights and view opposition as discriminatory.

Stable wage earners in secure employment. The majority of this married Finnish group works in regular employment with reliable income, allowing them to manage their household finances without significant stress.

Self-employed and business owners. A smaller segment runs their own businesses or work as self-employed professionals, experiencing variable income but generally maintaining adequate household financial stability.
Pensioners and retirees. A notable portion of married households includes pensioners whose fixed retirement income provides predictable but sometimes modest financial resources.
Households facing financial strain. A minority struggle with household income adequacy, including those receiving unemployment or social benefits, experiencing genuine difficulty managing expenses.

Affluent households with investment income. A very small segment enjoys substantial household resources from multiple income sources including investments and savings, living comfortably with financial security.
Daily internet users - primarily younger, employed, or digitally engaged Italians who use the internet constantly for work, social media, and personal activities across multiple devices.
Regular internet users - middle-aged adults who use the internet most days for work, news, and online services, though not with the constant engagement of daily users.
Moderate internet users - older adults or those with limited digital needs who use the internet a few times a week for specific purposes like email, banking, or information seeking.
Occasional internet users - primarily elderly or digitally disconnected individuals who only occasionally go online, often requiring assistance or having limited interest in digital tools.
Non-internet users - a small segment of older Italians or those with strong resistance to digital technology who never use the internet.

Progressive urban Dutch adults who embrace modern living arrangements. They have lived with partners outside marriage as a normal part of their life trajectory and see cohabitation as a practical and socially acceptable choice.

Traditionally-minded Dutch adults, often married or from more conservative backgrounds, who have not lived with partners outside marriage. They view marriage as the appropriate framework for cohabitation, though they are not hostile to those who make different choices.

Younger Dutch adults in their first serious relationships who are currently cohabiting without marriage. They see this as a natural step before or instead of marriage and represent the normalized acceptance of this lifestyle in contemporary Netherlands.

Middle-aged Dutch adults who cohabited earlier in life but later married their partners. They have personal experience with unmarried cohabitation and view it as a legitimate life choice they themselves pursued.

Older or religiously-observant Dutch adults who have never cohabited outside marriage and hold more conservative views on this matter. While a small minority, they represent the traditional perspective that remains present in Dutch society.

Socially engaged professionals and activists who are religiously affiliated, comfortable with their income, and actively participate in civic organizations and associations as part of their regular engagement with community life.
Regular internet users who are coping financially and maintain some community involvement through organizations, though their participation is moderate rather than intensive.
Religiously observant individuals who are focused on family and personal responsibilities, with limited time or inclination for organizational work outside their immediate circles.
Secular or non-religious Poles who are economically stable and digitally active but prioritize individual pursuits and informal social connections over formal organizational membership.
Economically struggling individuals with limited resources and time, who rarely participate in formal organizations due to financial constraints and competing daily demands.

Politically engaged centrists and moderate left-leaning voters who feel a clear affinity with established parties like LREM, PS, or Les Verts. They follow politics regularly and have developed stable party preferences.
Skeptical moderates who don't strongly identify with any particular party, viewing them all as somewhat distant from their concerns. They may vote strategically but lack genuine partisan attachment.
Right-leaning or conservative voters with stronger party identification, likely aligned with LR or similar center-right parties. They tend to have clearer political convictions and party loyalty.

Disengaged or disillusioned citizens who feel alienated from mainstream politics and don't identify with any established party. They may be frustrated with the political system or simply uninterested in party politics.
Far-right or populist-leaning voters with strong identification toward RN (National Rally), representing a distinct political orientation outside the traditional centrist consensus.

Progressive majority who strongly reject shame about LGBTQ+ family members. This group has internalized Iceland's strong social acceptance of LGBTQ+ rights and views such shame as fundamentally wrong.

Moderate acceptors with some residual discomfort. They wouldn't feel ashamed but experience mild social awkwardness or uncertainty, reflecting a small minority who haven't fully embraced the progressive consensus.

Conflicted individuals who are genuinely uncertain about their feelings. They neither strongly agree nor disagree, possibly due to generational or cultural tensions between traditional and modern values.
Conservative dissenters who would feel some shame or discomfort. This small group holds traditional values that conflict with Iceland's dominant progressive stance on LGBTQ+ issues.
Strong traditionalists who would feel significant shame. This tiny minority holds deeply conservative views that are substantially at odds with Icelandic social norms.
Disengaged retirees with limited digital literacy who see no need for further skill development at this stage of life and rarely use the internet.
Moderately active retirees who occasionally use the internet and may pursue learning for personal enrichment or hobbies, but not for work-related purposes.
Digitally engaged retirees who use the internet daily and maintain intellectual curiosity, regularly taking courses or attending lectures on topics of interest.
Recently retired professionals who still maintain some work-related engagement or consulting activities and continue professional development out of habit or necessity.
Socially active retirees who attend lectures and conferences primarily for social connection and community engagement rather than skill improvement.

Pragmatic moderates who neither approve nor disapprove of unmarried cohabitation and childbearing. They view these as personal choices without strong moral judgment, reflecting Bulgaria's growing secularization.

Progressive approvers who support a woman/man having a child with an unmarried partner. They believe family structures beyond traditional marriage are acceptable and increasingly normal in modern society.

Traditional disapprovers who strongly disapprove or disapprove of having children outside marriage. They hold conservative values rooted in Orthodox Christian tradition and believe marriage should precede childbearing.
Enthusiastic progressives who strongly approve of unmarried couples having children together. They actively embrace non-traditional family arrangements as valid lifestyle choices.
Conflicted conservatives who disapprove but are not strongly opposed, reflecting uncertainty between traditional values and awareness of changing social norms in Bulgaria.

Women from working-class backgrounds whose mothers were employed as wage workers, reflecting the common pattern of maternal employment in post-communist Poland during their childhood in the early 2000s.
Women whose mothers were not working during their adolescence, either due to caregiving responsibilities, unemployment, or early retirement—a significant minority experience in Poland.
Women whose mothers were self-employed or ran small businesses, representing the entrepreneurial segment of Polish society during that period.
Women who experienced the absence or death of their mother during adolescence, a smaller but meaningful group with distinct family circumstances.
Women with uncertain or unclear memories of their mother's employment status during childhood, or those from complex family situations that don't fit neatly into standard categories.

Daily internet users for work and personal life. These are primarily employed professionals who rely on internet connectivity for their jobs and use it extensively throughout the day across multiple devices.
Regular but not constant users who access the internet most days for work purposes and some personal use, but don't feel compelled to be online constantly.
Moderate users who go online a few times a week, typically for specific work tasks or occasional personal needs, representing those with less intensive work requirements.
Occasional users who rarely need internet access, either working in roles with minimal digital requirements or having limited personal interest in online activities.
Non-users or those who never use the internet, a very small segment likely consisting of older workers or those in traditional occupations with no digital component.
Non-unionized workers with limited education who have never engaged with union membership, viewing it as irrelevant to their work situation or lacking awareness of union benefits.
Former union members from earlier in their careers who were previously organized but have since left the workforce or changed to non-union employment.
Currently active union members, primarily in traditional sectors or public employment, who maintain membership for workplace protection and collective bargaining.
Self-employed or informal workers with lower secondary education who operate outside formal employment structures where union membership would apply.
Young workers or those in precarious employment who are aware of unions but face barriers to membership due to job instability or employer resistance.

Pragmatic centrists who feel connected to mainstream parties. These individuals, often with stable employment or union backgrounds, see value in identifying with established political parties that represent their economic interests and social concerns.

Disengaged skeptics without strong party affiliation. Skeptical of political institutions and parties, they prefer to evaluate issues independently rather than commit to a particular party, reflecting broader Hungarian political fragmentation.

Conservative traditionalists aligned with right-wing parties. Holding traditional values on social issues, they feel a clear affinity with conservative or nationalist parties that reflect their worldview on family, religion, and national identity.

Progressive liberals supporting left-leaning or centrist parties. Socially liberal on issues like cohabitation and secular values, they identify with parties promoting progressive policies and democratic institutions.

Economically anxious voters seeking representation. Struggling with household finances, they feel drawn to parties promising economic relief or change, though their loyalty may be conditional on perceived results.

Rural workers with stable employment in agriculture, small businesses, or local services who have never engaged with formal union structures, viewing them as irrelevant to their work context or as urban/industrial institutions.
Older residents who were previously members of unions during their working years in more formal employment sectors but have since retired or left the workforce.

Younger or middle-aged individuals in precarious or informal work arrangements (seasonal labor, self-employment, small family businesses) who see little practical benefit or opportunity to join unions.
A small minority of residents employed in sectors with stronger union traditions (public sector, larger employers) who maintain or have maintained union membership as a normal part of employment.
Ideologically skeptical individuals who view unions negatively due to cultural conservatism or distrust of collective organizations, actively rejecting membership.

Urban progressives and cohabitation-experienced Finns: Young to middle-aged, often university-educated, living in cities. They have personal experience with cohabitation, strongly approve of unmarried partnerships, and view this as a normal life choice. They answer 'Yes' readily.

Pragmatic mainstream Finns: Middle-aged, employed, moderately liberal on social issues. They approve or are neutral about cohabitation and may have cohabited themselves or know many who have. They answer 'Yes' without hesitation.

Traditional or religiously-minded Finns: Older or more conservative, married or long-married, with traditional values. They disapprove of cohabitation but acknowledge it happens widely in modern Finland. They answer 'No' but recognize the practice is common.

Younger never-cohabited Finns: Young adults who haven't yet lived with a partner, either due to age, relationship status, or personal preference. They may approve of cohabitation in principle but have no personal experience. They answer 'No' factually.

Trade union members and working-class Finns: Employed in manual or service work, moderate social attitudes. They have moderate approval of cohabitation and some personal experience. They answer 'Yes' or 'No' depending on personal history.

Pragmatic wage earners with moderate civic engagement. These employed individuals trust institutional authorities like national regulatory bodies and view vaccination as a practical health measure aligned with social responsibility. They represent the mainstream of Swiss society.

Cautious skeptics who respect regulatory approval but want more time or information before deciding. They are not opposed to vaccination in principle but prefer to observe outcomes in others first before committing.

Vaccine-hesitant individuals with concerns about safety, speed of development, or personal autonomy. Despite living in a country with strong regulatory institutions, they distrust the vaccination program or have ideological objections to medical mandates.

Early adopters and health-conscious individuals who have already been vaccinated or are eager to do so. They view vaccination as both a personal health benefit and a civic duty to protect their community.

Disengaged individuals with low civic participation who have not thought carefully about the question or lack access to reliable information. Their responses may be unstable or influenced by immediate social context.
Retired or semi-retired professionals who have stepped back from active career development and see little need for work-related training at this stage of life.
Actively employed workers in skilled positions who regularly engage in professional development and training to maintain competitiveness in their fields.
Self-employed or small business owners who selectively pursue training when they identify specific skill gaps relevant to their business needs.
Workers in transitional career phases or those seeking to adapt to changing workplace demands who view training as necessary for job security.
Individuals in lower-skilled or routine positions with limited employer-sponsored training opportunities and minimal personal motivation for skill development.
Healthy individuals with minimal medical needs who rarely require treatment and thus haven't experienced waiting list issues
People with occasional medical needs who accessed treatment without significant delays, either through private healthcare or timely public system access
Individuals with chronic or ongoing health conditions who have experienced delays in receiving needed medical treatment due to long waiting lists in the public system
Affluent Australians who primarily use private healthcare and have largely avoided public system waiting lists
People uncertain about their healthcare experiences or reluctant to categorize their situation clearly
Devout believers in Catholic faith who accept miracles as real manifestations of divine intervention in the world, common in rural Philippine communities with strong church presence.
Moderate believers who think miracles probably happen but maintain some skepticism, representing those with faith but influenced by modern education or exposure to alternative explanations.
Skeptics who doubt miracles occur in the way traditionally described, though they may not completely reject the possibility, reflecting growing secular influence even in villages.
Uncertain individuals who genuinely cannot decide whether miracles are real, often younger people or those with mixed religious and secular worldviews.
Firm disbelievers who reject miracles as supernatural events, though this group is smallest given the strong Catholic cultural context of rural Philippines.

Religious followers who believe their faith treats genders equally. This group is predominantly Christian (given Suriname's religious composition) and interprets their religious teachings as supporting gender equality, even if they acknowledge some traditional gender roles.

Religious adherents who recognize their religion treats men better than women. They acknowledge traditional patriarchal structures within their faith but may accept this as part of religious doctrine or cultural practice.

Non-religious or secular individuals who don't belong to any religion. This group is substantial in Suriname and simply cannot answer based on religious teachings, making option A their natural choice.

Spiritual but non-religious people who either see gender equality in spiritual frameworks or are uncertain how to evaluate this question without formal religious affiliation. They may lean toward equality or express uncertainty.

Uncertain or conflicted respondents who struggle to assess their religion's stance on gender equality or who recognize complexity in the question. They may select 'can't choose' or express ambivalence.
Secular skeptics who reject religious concepts entirely. They don't believe in God, don't believe in heaven/hell, and are skeptical of miracles and life after death.

Agnostic pragmatists uncertain about metaphysical claims. They're unsure about God's existence and tend to be uncertain or skeptical about afterlife beliefs, reflecting their broader epistemic caution.

Spiritual but not religious believers who accept a Higher Power but maintain distance from traditional doctrine. They're somewhat open to life after death as part of a broader spiritual worldview, though not dogmatically.
Doubting believers with residual faith. They believe in God despite doubts and maintain some openness to afterlife concepts, though with less certainty than committed believers.
Committed religious believers with traditional faith. They know God exists without doubt and are likely to believe in life after death as part of their coherent religious worldview.

Middle-of-the-road pragmatists who see themselves as average members of society with modest means and stability. They place themselves squarely in the middle of the social scale, viewing their position as neither privileged nor disadvantaged.

Skeptical or uncertain respondents who struggle to position themselves on an abstract social hierarchy and may distrust the premise of the question. They are hesitant to make definitive claims about their social standing.

Working-class individuals who perceive themselves as below the middle of the social scale due to economic constraints and limited opportunities in small-town Russia. They acknowledge their position as lower-middle or lower on the hierarchy.

Relatively successful or educated residents who view themselves as above average in their small-town context, placing themselves in the upper-middle range. They may work in professional roles or have better economic security than their peers.

Marginalized or struggling individuals who see themselves at the bottom of the social scale due to unemployment, poverty, or social exclusion. They have a clear sense of disadvantage relative to others in their community.
Religious believers with spiritual conviction. These individuals actively practice a religion and consider themselves spiritual, viewing their faith as central to their identity and worldview.
Secular non-spiritual individuals. These people explicitly reject both organized religion and spiritual beliefs, preferring a materialist or rationalist perspective on life.
Spiritual but non-religious seekers. These individuals pursue spiritual meaning and connection outside of formal religious institutions, often drawing from multiple traditions or personal philosophy.
Religious practitioners without spiritual emphasis. These people follow a religion for cultural, family, or community reasons but don't strongly identify as spiritual persons.
Uncertain or undecided individuals. These people struggle to categorize themselves clearly across these dimensions and prefer not to commit to a single description.
Secular skeptics with no religious belief. They don't believe in God and are skeptical of miracles, viewing them as natural phenomena misinterpreted or explained by science.
Agnostic pragmatists who are uncertain about religious matters generally. They can't decide on miracles and remain open but unconvinced, reflecting their broader uncertainty about spiritual claims.
Moderate believers with some faith in God and openness to miracles. They probably believe miracles are possible but aren't certain, reflecting a cautious approach to religious claims.
